title: Explain all the types of SQL joins.
shortTitle: Explain all the types of SQL joins.
topicTitle: Joins — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS

s1_definition.profdef: SQL joins combine rows from two tables based on a related column. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. A LEFT (OUTER) JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching right rows, filling nulls where there is no match. A RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN is the mirror, keeping all right rows. A FULL (OUTER) JOIN returns all rows from both, matched where possible and null-filled otherwise. A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product of every left row with every right row. A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India matching accounts to transactions. An INNER JOIN shows only accounts that have at least one transaction — anyone with no activity is left out. A LEFT JOIN shows every account including dormant ones, with blanks where there are no transactions. A RIGHT JOIN would keep every transaction even if its account record were somehow missing. A FULL JOIN shows everything from both sides. A CROSS JOIN pairs every account with every promotional offer to build all possible combinations. A SELF JOIN is used when matching rows within one table, like pairing each employee with their manager who is also in the employees table.
s1_definition.oneliner: INNER keeps matches only, LEFT and RIGHT keep all of one side, FULL keeps all of both, CROSS pairs everything with everything, and SELF joins a table to itself.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SQL joins combine rows from two tables based on a related column. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. A LEFT (OUTER) JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching right rows, filling nulls where there is no match. A RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN is the mirror, keeping all right rows. A FULL (OUTER) JOIN returns all rows from both, matched where possible and null-filled otherwise. A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product of every left row with every right row. A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India matching accounts to transactions. An INNER JOIN shows only accounts that have at least one transaction — anyone with no activity is left out. A LEFT JOIN shows every account including dormant ones, with blanks where there are no transactions. A RIGHT JOIN would keep every transaction even if its account record were somehow missing. A FULL JOIN shows everything from both sides. A CROSS JOIN pairs every account with every promotional offer to build all possible combinations. A SELF JOIN is used when matching rows within one table, like pairing each employee with their manager who is also in the employees table.

**One line to remember:** INNER keeps matches only, LEFT and RIGHT keep all of one side, FULL keeps all of both, CROSS pairs everything with everything, and SELF joins a table to itself.

sections.s2_technical:
An INNER JOIN is the default and most common. It returns only the rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables, so unmatched rows on either side disappear. Joining accounts to transactions with an inner join lists only accounts that actually have transactions, dropping dormant accounts. You write it as `FROM accounts a JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id`.

A LEFT OUTER JOIN, usually written just LEFT JOIN, returns every row from the left table regardless of whether it matches, and fills the right-side columns with null where there is no match. This is how you find "all accounts and their transactions, including accounts with none" — the dormant accounts appear with null transaction columns. A powerful variant is the anti-join: a LEFT JOIN with a `WHERE right_table.key IS NULL` returns exactly the left rows that have no match, such as accounts that have never transacted. A RIGHT OUTER JOIN is the exact mirror, keeping all rows from the right table and null-filling the left; in practice people rarely use RIGHT JOIN because you can always reorder the tables and write a LEFT JOIN, which reads more naturally.

A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching them where the condition holds and null-filling wherever a row on one side has no partner on the other. It is useful for reconciliation, such as comparing two systems' records to find entries present in one but not the other on either side. A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product: every row of the left table paired with every row of the right table, so two tables of sizes m and n yield m times n rows. It has no join condition and is used deliberately to generate combinations, for example pairing every account with every available product to seed a matrix, but it is dangerous by accident because an unintended cross join on large tables explodes the result.

A SELF JOIN is not a separate syntax but a technique: you join a table to itself using table aliases, which is how you relate rows within the same table. The classic example is an employees table where each row has a manager id pointing at another row in the same table, and you self-join to list each employee alongside their manager's name. Two more concepts round out the picture. An equi-join is any join whose condition uses equality, which covers almost all everyday joins, while a non-equi join uses ranges or inequalities, for example joining a transaction to a fee-tier table where the amount falls between a tier's lower and upper bounds. A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins on all columns with the same name in both tables, which is concise but risky because adding a same-named column later silently changes the join, so most teams avoid it in favor of explicit `ON` conditions. A senior nuance is performance: joins are driven by the optimizer choosing among nested-loop, hash, and merge join strategies, indexes on the join columns are critical, and outer joins can be more expensive because the database must preserve unmatched rows; you should also be careful that filters in the `WHERE` clause on an outer-joined table can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into an inner join unless you move the condition into the `ON` clause.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs a statement listing only accounts that had transactions, which is an INNER JOIN, and separately a dormancy report listing all accounts including those with no transactions, which is a LEFT JOIN, with the never-transacted accounts found by the anti-join pattern.

Problem 2 — The reconciliation team compares two ledgers to find entries present in one but missing from the other on either side, which is a FULL OUTER JOIN. The marketing team wants every account paired with every offer to build a campaign matrix, which is a CROSS JOIN. The HR view needs each employee next to their manager from the same table, which is a SELF JOIN.

The mini-project runs an INNER, LEFT (with anti-join), FULL, CROSS, and SELF join over small banking tables and a Java reporter that logs each result so the differences are visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: accounts SAV2001 and CUR3001 (each with a transaction) and SAV2099 (dormant), transactions T1, T2, and T3 (T3 has a null account_id), two offers, and three employees where Rajesh and Priya report to Anil.

Step 1 (INNER): The database matches each account to transactions on account_id. SAV2001 matches T1 and CUR3001 matches T2. SAV2099 has no transaction and T3 has no real account, so both are dropped. The result has two rows.

Step 2 (LEFT): The database keeps every account. SAV2001 and CUR3001 pair with their transactions, and dormant SAV2099 appears with a null txn_id. The result has three rows, showing the dormant account.

Step 3 (LEFT anti-join): Adding `WHERE t.txn_id IS NULL` keeps only the left rows with no match, returning exactly SAV2099 — the never-transacted account.

Step 4 (FULL): The database keeps all accounts and all transactions. SAV2001 and CUR3001 match, dormant SAV2099 appears with null txn, and the orphan-ish T3 with null account_id appears with a null account id. Both unmatched sides are preserved.

Step 5 (CROSS): With no condition, every account pairs with every offer. Three accounts times two offers yields six rows — the Cartesian product used to build a campaign matrix.

Step 6 (SELF): The employees table is joined to itself, matching each employee's manager_id to another employee's emp_id. Rajesh and Priya show manager Anil, and Anil shows a null manager because he is the head.

```text
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - INNER (accounts WITH txns) -> [SAV2001|T1, CUR3001|T2]
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - LEFT (all accounts, dormant=NULL) -> [SAV2001|T1, CUR3001|T2, SAV2099|null]
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - LEFT ANTI (never transacted) -> [SAV2099]
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - FULL OUTER (both sides) -> [SAV2001|T1, CUR3001|T2, SAV2099|null, null|T3]
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - CROSS (account × offer) -> [SAV2001|CB5, SAV2001|EMI0, CUR3001|CB5, CUR3001|EMI0, SAV2099|CB5, SAV2099|EMI0]
Feb 14,2026 13:00:00 INFO  JoinsDao - SELF (employee + manager) -> [Anil (Head)|null, Rajesh|Anil (Head), Priya|Anil (Head)]
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```text

  INNER  → only matches              → SAV2001|T1, CUR3001|T2
  LEFT   → all accounts, null right  → +SAV2099|null

```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — SQL Join Types ═══

  ┌─ All join types ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ INNER        : rows matching in BOTH                             │
  │ LEFT OUTER   : all LEFT + matched right (null-fill)              │
  │ RIGHT OUTER  : all RIGHT + matched left (mirror of LEFT)         │
  │ FULL OUTER   : all from BOTH, null-fill unmatched either side    │
  │ CROSS        : Cartesian product (m×n), no condition             │
  │ SELF         : table joined to itself via aliases               │
  │ equi vs non-equi: = condition vs range/BETWEEN condition         │
  │ NATURAL      : auto-match same-named cols (risky, avoid)         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Pitfalls / performance ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHERE on outer side turns LEFT into INNER → put it in ON         │
  │ accidental CROSS on big tables explodes rows                     │
  │ index join columns; optimizer picks nested-loop/hash/merge       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Decision ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  only matches            → INNER
  keep all of one table   → LEFT (reorder instead of RIGHT)
  find non-matches        → LEFT + WHERE right IS NULL (anti-join)
  reconcile both sides    → FULL
  all combinations        → CROSS
  relate rows same table  → SELF
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SQL joins combine rows from two tables on a related column, and there are a handful of types that differ in which unmatched rows they keep. An INNER JOIN, the default, returns only rows that match in both tables, so unmatched rows on either side disappear — joining accounts to transactions with an inner join lists only accounts that actually transacted. A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns every row from the left table and null-fills the right where there is no match, which is how you list all accounts including dormant ones; and the anti-join pattern, a LEFT JOIN with a `WHERE right.key IS NULL`, returns exactly the left rows with no match, such as accounts that never transacted. A RIGHT OUTER JOIN is the mirror, keeping all right rows, though in practice people reorder the tables and write a LEFT JOIN because it reads more naturally.

A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matched where possible and null-filled otherwise, which is ideal for reconciliation when you need entries present in either system but missing from the other. A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product, pairing every left row with every right row with no condition, useful deliberately to build combinations like every account by every offer, but dangerous by accident because it explodes on large tables. A SELF JOIN is a technique rather than new syntax: you join a table to itself with aliases to relate rows within the same table, the classic case being an employees table where each row's manager id points at another employee.

Two refinements complete the picture: an equi-join uses an equality condition, which covers almost everything, while a non-equi join uses ranges, like matching an amount to a fee tier with a `BETWEEN`, and a NATURAL JOIN auto-joins on same-named columns, which is concise but risky so most teams prefer explicit `ON`. The senior pitfalls I always mention are that a filter on an outer-joined table placed in `WHERE` silently turns a LEFT JOIN back into an inner join unless you move it into the `ON` clause, and that indexes on join columns are critical because the optimizer chooses among nested-loop, hash, and merge strategies. At the National Bank of India we use INNER joins for statements, LEFT anti-joins for dormancy reports, FULL joins for ledger reconciliation, CROSS joins for campaign matrices, and SELF joins for the org hierarchy. The line I always state is that INNER keeps matches only, LEFT and RIGHT keep all of one side, FULL keeps all of both, CROSS pairs everything with everything, and SELF joins a table to itself.
